newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Over 4,000 journalists set to invade HK for handover.
newsitem.headline: Over 4,000 journalists set to invade HK for handover.

text.p: At least 4,000 journalists from the world's media are set to invade Hong Kong for one of the last great spectacles of the 20th Century, the British colony's historic handover to China.
The Hong Kong government had been inundated with more than 4,000 applications for accreditation from more than 350 news organisations, spokesman Jonathan Lange told Reuters on Tuesday.
Lange said applications were likely to continue arriving even though Monday was the official cutoff date.
The Hong Kong government was prepared to deal with an influx of up to 6,000 journalists for the event, Lange said.
"We have been sort of anticipating around about 6,000. We've been working on the basis that there could be up to 6,000.
"The media centre that we are setting up at the Convention and Exhibition Centre should be able to cater for that."
The centre's new extension, jutting into the sea along the Wanchai waterfront like a giant clam, is the venue for official handover celebrations including a joint Sino-British flag-changing ceremony.

China resumes sovereignty over Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, ending more than 150 years of British colonial rule and Chinese national shame over the territory, prised away from Beijing during the 19th century opium wars.
China has agreed to let the Hong Kong government, which is to keep a high degree of autonomy after the takeover, to handle the media invasion without any interference.
China and Britain have worked out the broad outlines of a 3,200-strong VIP guest list.
About 400 "international guests" would be included. Some would be government ministers and the heads of big international organisations, a British official said last week.
Britain is sending heir to the throne Prince Charles to Hong Kong on the final voyage of the royal yacht Brittania to preside over Britain's farewell to the colony.
China's President Jiang Zemin is expected to appear, but possibly not until after the British Union Jack has been furled and the red Chinese flag has been hoisted.

A myriad of events ranging from fireworks displays and carnivals to open-air variety shows, operas and food festivals is also planned by local organisations and businesses keen to cash in on the merrymaking.
Hong Kong's tourism industry is expecting a flood of visitors curious to get a glimpse of history in the making in this territory of 6.4 million people.
